title: Navigating Without Instruments
sourceNote: Bài viết gốc theo phong cách IELTS Academic Reading; dữ kiện tổng hợp từ tư liệu nhân học và lịch sử hàng hải Thái Bình Dương.

sections.text: The islands of Polynesia are scattered across a vast triangle of the Pacific Ocean, with Hawaii at its northern point, New Zealand in the south-west and Easter Island in the east. The distances between them are enormous; some groups of islands lie thousands of kilometres from their nearest neighbours. Yet by around eight hundred years ago, almost every habitable island within this triangle had been settled, making it one of the last regions on earth to be reached by human beings. How the ancestors of the Polynesians found these tiny specks of land in such an immense ocean has long fascinated scholars. Their ancestors are thought to have come originally from island South-East Asia, moving gradually eastwards over thousands of years.

For much of the twentieth century, many Western scholars doubted that such voyages could have been made deliberately. In 1956, the historian Andrew Sharp argued that the islands had been settled largely by accident, by canoes blown off course by storms or carried by currents while their crews were fishing or travelling between nearby islands. In his view, navigation without instruments was simply too unreliable for voyagers to find distant islands on purpose and then return home. His argument was influential, although it angered many Pacific Islanders, whose oral traditions described planned voyages of discovery.

Evidence against the accidental theory gradually accumulated. In the early 1970s, researchers used computers to simulate thousands of drifting voyages, taking into account winds and currents. Hardly any of the simulated canoes reached Hawaii, New Zealand or Easter Island by chance, suggesting that these remote islands could only have been settled by people who were sailing in a chosen direction. Archaeologists also found that the settlers had brought with them the plants and animals they needed to establish new communities, including pigs, dogs, chickens and crops such as taro, which hardly seemed consistent with accidental arrivals.

The most dramatic test came in 1976. A group of enthusiasts in Hawaii built a replica of a traditional double-hulled voyaging canoe, which they named Hōkūleʻa, and set out to sail it to Tahiti, more than four thousand kilometres to the south, without compass, charts or other modern instruments. Since no Hawaiian still possessed the knowledge needed, they recruited Mau Piailug, a master navigator from a small island in Micronesia, where traditional methods had survived. After about a month at sea, the canoe reached Tahiti, where it was greeted by a crowd of thousands. The route was the same one described in Hawaiian traditions.

Traditional navigators rely on a detailed knowledge of the sky. They memorise the points on the horizon where particular stars rise and set, so that a star rising in a known position can be used to hold a course; as one star climbs too high to be useful, the navigator switches to another rising at the same point. During the day, the sun serves a similar purpose. Navigators also learn which stars pass directly overhead at particular islands, which helps them judge how far north or south they have travelled.

The ocean provides further clues. Large swells, generated by distant weather systems, travel in consistent directions for long periods, and an experienced navigator can feel the pattern of several swells through the movement of the canoe, even at night or under cloud. Near land, swells bend around islands and bounce off them, creating patterns that reveal an island's position before it can be seen. Clouds tend to gather above islands, and some seabirds, which fly out to sea to feed during the day and return to land at dusk, indicate the direction of land to those who know their habits.

The success of Hōkūleʻa inspired a revival of traditional voyaging across the Pacific. One of the Hawaiian crew members, Nainoa Thompson, studied with Mau Piailug and in 1980 navigated the canoe to Tahiti and back himself, becoming the first Hawaiian in centuries to make such a voyage using traditional methods. Since then, voyaging societies have trained new generations of navigators, and Hōkūleʻa has sailed around the world. For many Pacific Islanders, the revival has become a powerful symbol of cultural pride, demonstrating the skill and courage of the people who first explored the ocean.

explain.B: Đoạn B: Andrew Sharp cho rằng các đảo được định cư chủ yếu do tình cờ, vì thuyền bị bão thổi lệch hướng → một giả thuyết về việc định cư tình cờ: {h}.
explain.C: Đoạn C: mô phỏng máy tính cho thấy hầu như không thuyền trôi dạt nào tới được các đảo xa; người định cư mang theo cây trồng và vật nuôi → bằng chứng các chuyến đi có kế hoạch: {h}.
explain.D: Đoạn D: năm 1976, thuyền phục dựng Hōkūleʻa đi từ Hawaii tới Tahiti không dùng dụng cụ → một chuyến đi hiện đại kiểm chứng phương pháp cũ: {h}. Đoạn chỉ nói thuyền là bản phục dựng, không mô tả cách đóng thuyền, nên không phải {i:6}.
explain.E: Đoạn E: ghi nhớ điểm mọc và lặn của các ngôi sao để giữ hướng → dùng sao để giữ hướng đi: {h}.
explain.F: Đoạn F: sóng lừng, sóng phản xạ quanh đảo, mây tụ trên đảo, chim biển → đọc dấu hiệu từ biển và bầu trời: {h}.
explain.G: Đoạn G: Nainoa Thompson học từ Mau Piailug, các hội hàng hải đào tạo thế hệ mới → phục hưng một truyền thống: {h}.

items.q: Which TWO pieces of evidence suggested that the islands were not settled by accident?
options: Computer simulations showed drifting canoes rarely reached the most remote islands.
Settlers had brought useful animals and plants with them.
Ancient maps of the islands were discovered in Tahiti.
European sailors reported seeing Polynesian fleets.
Canoes from the period were found buried on Easter Island.
items.e: Đoạn C: mô phỏng máy tính cho thấy 'Hardly any of the simulated canoes reached' Hawaii, New Zealand hay đảo Phục Sinh, và người định cư mang theo lợn, chó, gà, khoai sọ. Các phương án còn lại (bản đồ cổ, thủy thủ châu Âu, thuyền chôn) không có trong bài.

items.q: Which TWO natural signs can show navigators that land is near?
options: seabirds flying back to land in the evening
a sudden fall in the temperature of the sea
the colour of the water changing to red
items.e: Đoạn F: 'Clouds tend to gather above islands', và chim biển ra khơi kiếm ăn ban ngày rồi 'return to land at dusk' cho biết hướng đất liền. Nhiệt độ nước hay màu nước không được nhắc tới.

items.q: A star rising in a known position helps the navigator to hold a ______
items.e: Đoạn E: 'a star rising in a known position can be used to hold a course' – giữ hướng đi → course.

items.q: During the day, the ______ is used in a similar way to the stars
items.e: Đoạn E: 'During the day, the sun serves a similar purpose' → sun.

items.q: Navigators can feel the pattern of several ______ through the movement of the canoe
items.e: Đoạn F: hoa tiêu giàu kinh nghiệm 'can feel the pattern of several swells through the movement of the canoe' → swells.
